paragraphs: Nature sets limits to the stature of a well-formed man and, beyond those limits, produces only giants or dwarfs. In the same way, for a State to have the best possible constitution, one can fix limits that keep it from being too large to be well governed and too small to maintain itself. Every body politic has a _maximum_ strength that it cannot exceed and that it only loses by growing larger. The more the social tie is stretched, the looser it becomes; and in general a small State is stronger, in proportion to its size, than a large one.

A thousand arguments support this principle. First, distance makes administration harder, the way a weight gets heavier at the end of a longer lever. The greater the distance, the heavier the burden of administration. That is because each city has its own administration, which the people pay for; each district has its own, which the people also pay for; then come the provinces, and then the great governments, the satrapies and viceroyalties, which cost more the higher you go, always at the expense of the unfortunate people. Last of all comes the supreme administration, which overshadows all the rest. All these added costs are a constant drain on the subjects. Far from being better governed by all these different levels, they are worse governed than they would be under a single authority. Meanwhile hardly any resources remain for emergencies, and when the State has to draw on them, it is always on the verge of ruin.

There is more. A distant government has less vigor and speed in making sure the laws are obeyed, in preventing nuisances, correcting abuses and stopping rebellious plots that begin in faraway places. The people, for their part, feel less affection for rulers they never see, for a country that looks to them like the whole world, and for fellow citizens most of whom are strangers. The same laws cannot suit so many different provinces, with their different customs, their widely varied climates, and their inability to bear a uniform government. Different laws only breed trouble and confusion among peoples who share the same rulers, stay in constant contact, mix and intermarry, and, coming under new customs, never know whether even their own inheritance is really theirs. Talent is buried, virtue goes unknown and vice goes unpunished, among such a multitude of men who do not know one another, crowded together at the seat of the central administration. The leaders, swamped with business, see nothing for themselves, and the State is run by clerks. Finally, the measures needed to maintain the general authority, which all those distant officials either want to evade or want to deceive, use up all the energy of the public, so that none is left for the happiness of the people. There is barely enough to defend it when the need comes, and so a body too big for its constitution collapses, crushed under its own weight.

Again, the State must give itself a secure foundation if it is to be stable, to withstand the shocks it cannot help suffering, and to bear the efforts it will be forced to make to sustain itself. For all peoples have a kind of centrifugal force that makes them constantly act against one another and tend to grow at their neighbors’ expense, like the vortices of Descartes. The weak therefore risk being swallowed up soon, and it is almost impossible for any State to preserve itself except by putting itself in a kind of equilibrium with all the others, so that the pressure on it is practically equal on every side.

So there are reasons to expand and reasons to contract, and it takes no small skill in a statesman to find, between them, the middle course that best preserves the State. It may be said that the reason for expansion, being only external and relative, should rank below the reasons for contraction, which are internal and absolute. The first thing to look for is a strong and healthy constitution, and it is better to rely on the vigor that good government produces than on the resources of a large territory.

It may be added that some States are known to have been constituted so that the need to make conquests was built into their very constitution, and that to survive they had to expand without end. Perhaps they congratulated themselves greatly on this lucky necessity. Yet it showed them, together with the limit of their greatness, the unavoidable moment of their fall.
